messages.subject: Calculating continuous interpolation of excursion functions for LGCP
messages.subject_clean: Calculating continuous interpolation of excursion functions for LGCP
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have fitted a LGCP model with some simulated data and I was using the 'continuous' function in the 'excursion' package to obtain the excursion funtion.

But with different iteration of simulation, there are some iteration where the 'continuous' function is stuck. Normally it only takes about couple of seconds to get the result, but in some iteration, the computation just seems to freeze.

I can't figure out the reason for this and I hope there can be some clarification. Moreover, if there is any way to terminate the computation if it freezes.

Thanks!
David

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Calculating continuous interpolation of excursion functions for LGCP
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
My best guess is that you’re running into a problematic geometry issue in the continuous excursion construction; I believe we haven’t fully worked around a problem where it couldn’t handle two boundary triangles meeting at a single vertex only (since the resulting triangulation wouldn’t have proper manifold connectivity). But I don’t remember if that would cause it to freeze or to crash.
Check the list of running processes when it appears to freeze to see if it’s stuck in R or in an external process (which would likely be “fmesher”). If it’s fmesher, terminate it and then run traceback() in the R console and send here so I can see where it got stuck.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
This looks like a really weird bug; the code calls inla.mesh.create internally with input objects that are identical to those in the original mesh (indicating that the whole mesh should form the excursion set) but it freezes when doing that, but calling the same function using the objects from the mesh object directly doesn't cause a freeze. It _does_ however produce a different mesh than intended, since it contains an extension, which _may_ be due to omitting an extend=FALSE argument, but adding that argument doesn't fix the problem.
I'll need to debug further...

Finn

To partially work around it, you can set an fmesher timeout (in whole seconds), so that you get an error after a while instead of
having to abort it manually. If you wrap it in a tryCatch you can detect it automatically. To set the timeout, use something like
  inla.setOption(fmesher.timeout=10)
(for a 10 second limit on all fmesher calls; you may want to set a larger value)

Finn

...and the withTimeout option would not work for this, since fmesher is called via a system() call. From the withTimeout help text:

"System calls via system() and system2() cannot be timed out via the above mechanisms. However, in R (>= 3.5.0) these functions have argument timeout providing their own independent timeout mechanism."

The fmesher.timeout INLA option uses that new "own independent timeout mechanism".

Finn

I'm currently working on a new interface to the fmesher internal code that will allow user interrupt with Ctrl-C as well as with Timeout(), but that will take a while to be available.

messages.subject: Separating Cox PH model into test and training set? - error messages
messages.subject_clean: Separating Cox PH model into test and training set? - error messages
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm familiar with the process of coding the response variable as NA to split datasets into training and validation sets. I'm trying to do the same with a Cox PH model. The idea was:

gsplit <- sample(rep(0:1,each=4930)) # for dataset of 9860 rows
grid3@data$split <- gsplit # add this to my SpatialPolygons dataframe
grid3@data$status <- ifelse(grid3@data$split == 1, NA, grid3@data$status) # code half as NAs
survinla <- inla.surv(grid3@data$def_mean, grid3@data$status)

At this point I get the warning:
Warning message:
In inla.surv.1(time, event, time2, truncation, .special = .special) :
  Some elements in `event' are NA: set them to observed failures.

So I thought, maybe I can recode the attributes of the inla.surv object:

survinla$time <- ifelse(grid3@data$split == 1, NA, survinla$time)
survinla$lower <- ifelse(grid3@data$split == 1, NA, survinla$lower)
survinla$upper <- ifelse(grid3@data$split == 1, NA, survinla$upper)
survinla$event <- ifelse(grid3@data$split == 1, NA, survinla$event)
survinla$truncation <- ifelse(grid3@data$split == 1, NA, survinla$truncation)
lattice_temp <- poly2nb(grid3, row.names = grid3@data$id2)
nb2INLA(paste(getwd(), "/lattice.graph", sep = ""), lattice_temp)
lattice.adj <- paste(getwd(), "/lattice.graph", sep = "")
grid10 <- grid3@data # get a dataframe for INLA
inlacox <- inla(survinla ~ 1 + cost_mean + elev_mean + popn_mean + cop99 + PAs_mean + f(id2, model = "bym", graph = lattice.adj, scale.model = TRUE),
                data = grid10, family = "coxph",
                control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic=TRUE),
                control.hazard = list(model="rw1", n.intervals=20))

But this got me the error message:
Error in time[response$event == 1L] <- response$time[response$event ==  :
  NAs are not allowed in subscripted assignments

I've been experimenting with a binomial model + loglog link as an alternative, perhaps that would allow me to sidestep the recoding difficulty?

Best wishes,
Michael

messages.body_plain:
maybe check 'inla.coxph', as coxph is done by rewriting it as poisson
regression. for simple models, this conversion is done automatic, but
more complex ones, you might have to do that manually using
'inla.coxph'.

if a response is NA, then there is no (easy) way to predict a new
outcome as the poisson expansion is done based on the observed value.
you may have to do the prediction manually, using
'inla.posterior.sample', f.ex, to get a sample of the hazard function
and then compute the posterior of a new observation from that one.

H

messages.subject_clean: INLA binary install error on HPC cluster
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to install INLA on a Linux HPC cluster using inla.binary.install() command. However, I got the following error:

Error in download.file(map.filename(fnm), to.file, quiet = TRUE) :
  download from 'https://inla.r-inla-download.org/Linux-builds/./CentOS%20Linux-7%20(Core)/Version_21.02.23/64bit.tgz' failed
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In download.file(map.filename(fnm), to.file, quiet = TRUE) :
  downloaded length 4479790 != reported length 59788637
2: In download.file(map.filename(fnm), to.file, quiet = TRUE) :
  URL 'https://inla.r-inla-download.org/Linux-builds/CentOS%20Linux-7%20(Core)/Version_21.02.23/64bit.tgz': status was 'Failed writing received data to disk/application'

The issue is I can do the binary install of INLA if my R library directory is in the home/ directory. However, I got the above error when I change my R library to my own project/ directory. It is not recommended to put packages in home/ server directory as this will potentially cause issue when running jobs as the HPC cluster does not handle jobs run from the home/ directory. Is there any way to get around this? Or is this a issue of the HPC server? Thanks!

David

messages.subject: "Copy" function to estimate surveillance sensitivity?
messages.subject_clean: "Copy" function to estimate surveillance sensitivity?
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA discussion group,
I have some surveillance data for an infectious disease in space and time. The observations consist of positive or negative results for two types of surveillance. I would like to estimate the sensitivity of each surveillance method (which we can call Y and Z) by estimating a latent space-time infection probability. I found some examples on state-space modelling in INLA using the "copy" function and I thought this might be an appropriate approach. However, I made a toy example with a single location to test and I am not getting the results I expected. I wonder if you can tell me what I am doing wrong?

I'll define my simple model first.
I have an infection probability i_t which is a first-order random walk:

# i is the hidden infection status
# i_t = a_t * i_t-1 + o_t
# o_t ~ N(0,O)
# Temporal coefficient a_t is constant and equal to one
# Therefore
# 0 = i_t - i_t-1 - o_t [this is a first-order random walk]

# I have some observations from surveillance Y_t and Z_t  with ny_t and nz_t number of tests which have a constant sensitivity beta_Y and beta_Z to detect i_t, (0<=beta_Y<=1 and 0<=beta_Z<=1).

# observation model
# Y_t ~ Binomial(p_t, ny_t)
# logit(p_t) = beta_Y * i_t
# Z_t ~ Binomial(q_t, nz_t)
# logit(q_t) = beta_Z * i_t

# Following this framework, I simulate some data:

library(INLA)
library(boot)
library(foreach)

i<-(sin(seq(0,3.14*4,by=0.05)-3.14*0.5)+1)/2
t<-1:length(i)

beta_Y<-0.8
beta_Z<-0.4

n_Y<-rep(20,times=length(t))
pos_Y<-unlist(foreach(x=t)%do%rbinom(1,n_Y[x],i[x]*beta_Y))

n_Z<-rep(20,times=length(t))
pos_Z<-unlist(foreach(x=t)%do%rbinom(1,n_Z[x],i[x]*beta_Z))

# I then set up my data with three response variables, with the first column representing Y_t, the second Z_t, and the third column 0 = i_t - i_t-1 - o_t.

# Number of time steps
n<-max(t)
# Because i_t depends on i_t-1
m<-n-1
# Response matrix (first column Y_t, second column Z_t, third column 0)
resp<-matrix(NA, n+n+m, 3)
resp[1:n, 1]<- pos_Y
resp[(n+1):(n+n), 2]<- pos_Z
resp[(n+n+1):(n+n+m),3]<- 0

# Three likelihoods
fam<-c("binomial","binomial","gaussian")

num_trials<-c(n_Y,n_Z,rep(NA,m))

i1 = c(1:n,1:n,2:n)             # indices for i_t
j = c(rep(NA,n),rep(NA,n),2:n -1)    #indices for i_t-1
w1 = c(rep(NA,n),rep(NA,n), rep(-1,m)) # weight for -1 * o_t-1
l = c(rep(NA,n),rep(NA,n),2:n -1) # indices for o_t
w2 <- c(rep(NA,n),rep(NA,n), rep(-1,m)) # weight for  -1 * o_(t-1)
i2 = c(1:n,rep(NA,n),rep(NA,m))             # indices for i_t method Y
i3 = c(rep(NA,n),1:n,rep(NA,m))           # indices for i_t method Z

# Then I fit my model and plot the results:

mod.inla <- inla(resp ~ 0 +
                   f(i1, model = "iid",hyper = list(prec = list(initial = -10, fixed = TRUE)))+
                   f(j, w1, copy = "i1") + f(l, w2, model = "iid")+
                   f(i2, copy = "i1",hyper = list(beta = list(fixed = FALSE))) +
                   f(i3, copy = "i1",hyper = list(beta = list(fixed = FALSE))) ,
                 data = list(resp=resp, i1=i1, i2=i2, i3=i3, j=j, l=l, w1=w1, w2=w2), family = fam,
                 control.family = list(list(), list(),
                                       list(hyper = list(prec = list(initial = 10, fixed = TRUE)))),
                 control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                 Ntrials=num_trials
)

summary(mod.inla)

# Predicted response for Y compared to what I was expecting
matplot(mod.inla$summary.fitted.values[which(!is.na <http://is.na>(resp[,1])),c(1,3,5)],col=2,type="l",lty=c(1,2,2),ylim=c(0,1))
lines(t,i*beta_Y)

# Predicted response for Z compared to what I was expecting
matplot(mod.inla$summary.fitted.values[which(!is.na <http://is.na>(resp[,2])),c(1,3,5)],col=4,type="l",lty=c(1,2,2))
lines(t,i*beta_Z)

# Fitted i_t compared to true i_t
d<-mod.inla$summary.random$i1[,c(2,4,6)]
for(j in 1:3) d[,j]<-inv.logit(unlist(d[,j]))
matplot(d,col=3,type="l",lty=c(1,2,2),ylim=c(0,1))
lines(t,i)

# beta_Y and beta_Z (I think this is logit-linked?)
d<-mod.inla$summary.hyperpar[2:3,c(1,3,5)]
for(j in 1:3) d[,j]<-inv.logit(unlist(d[,j]))
d

# beta_Y compared to input
d<-inla.smarginal(mod.inla$marginals.hyperpar$`Beta for i2`)
d$x<-inv.logit(d$x)
plot(d,type="l",xlim=c(0,1))
abline(v=beta_Y,col=2)

# beta_Z compared to input
d<-inla.smarginal(mod.inla$marginals.hyperpar$`Beta for i3`)
d$x<-inv.logit(d$x)
plot(d,type="l",xlim=c(0,1))
abline(v=beta_Z,col=4)

Thanks in advance for your help and advice! Sorry if I have made some obvious mistakes - I am new to using INLA and have never used the "copy" functionality before.

Best,
Laura

>
> I'll define my simple model first.
> I have an infection probability i_t which is a first-order random
> walk:
>
> # i is the hidden infection status
> # i_t = a_t * i_t-1 + o_t
> # o_t ~ N(0,O)
> # Temporal coefficient a_t is constant and equal to one
> # Therefore
> # 0 = i_t - i_t-1 - o_t [this is a first-order random walk]
>
> # I have some observations from surveillance Y_t and Z_t  with ny_t
> and nz_t number of tests which have a constant sensitivity beta_Y and
> beta_Z to detect i_t, (0<=beta_Y<=1 and 0<=beta_Z<=1).
>
> # observation model
> # Y_t ~ Binomial(p_t, ny_t)
> # logit(p_t) = beta_Y * i_t
> # Z_t ~ Binomial(q_t, nz_t)
> # logit(q_t) = beta_Z * i_t
>
> # Following this framework, I simulate some data:
>
> library(INLA)
> library(boot)
> library(foreach)
>
> i<-(sin(seq(0,3.14*4,by=0.05)-3.14*0.5)+1)/2
> t<-1:length(i)
>
> beta_Y<-0.8
> beta_Z<-0.4
>
> n_Y<-rep(20,times=length(t))
> pos_Y<-unlist(foreach(x=t)%do%rbinom(1,n_Y[x],i[x]*beta_Y))
>
> n_Z<-rep(20,times=length(t))
> pos_Z<-unlist(foreach(x=t)%do%rbinom(1,n_Z[x],i[x]*beta_Z))
>
> # I then set up my data with three response variables, with the first
> column representing Y_t, the second Z_t, and the third column 0 = i_t
> - i_t-1 - o_t.
>
> # Number of time steps
> n<-max(t)
> # Because i_t depends on i_t-1
> m<-n-1
> # Response matrix (first column Y_t, second column Z_t, third column
> 0)
> resp<-matrix(NA, n+n+m, 3)
> resp[1:n, 1]<- pos_Y
> resp[(n+1):(n+n), 2]<- pos_Z
> resp[(n+n+1):(n+n+m),3]<- 0
>
> # Three likelihoods
> fam<-c("binomial","binomial","gaussian")
>
> num_trials<-c(n_Y,n_Z,rep(NA,m))
>
>
> i1 = c(1:n,1:n,2:n)             # indices for i_t
> j = c(rep(NA,n),rep(NA,n),2:n -1)    #indices for i_t-1
> w1 = c(rep(NA,n),rep(NA,n), rep(-1,m)) # weight for -1 * o_t-1
> l = c(rep(NA,n),rep(NA,n),2:n -1) # indices for o_t
> w2 <- c(rep(NA,n),rep(NA,n), rep(-1,m)) # weight for  -1 * o_(t-1)
> i2 = c(1:n,rep(NA,n),rep(NA,m))             # indices for i_t method Y
> i3 = c(rep(NA,n),1:n,rep(NA,m))           # indices for i_t method Z
>
> # Then I fit my model and plot the results:
>
> mod.inla <- inla(resp ~ 0 +
>                    f(i1, model = "iid",hyper = list(prec =
> list(initial = -10, fixed = TRUE)))+
>                    f(j, w1, copy = "i1") + f(l, w2, model = "iid")+
>                    f(i2, copy = "i1",hyper = list(beta = list(fixed =
> FALSE))) +
>                    f(i3, copy = "i1",hyper = list(beta = list(fixed =
> FALSE))) ,
>                  data = list(resp=resp, i1=i1, i2=i2, i3=i3, j=j, l=l,
> w1=w1, w2=w2), family = fam,
>                  control.family = list(list(), list(),
>                                        list(hyper = list(prec =
> list(initial = 10, fixed = TRUE)))),
>                  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
>                  Ntrials=num_trials
> )
>
> summary(mod.inla)
>
> # Predicted response for Y compared to what I was expecting
> matplot(mod.inla$summary.fitted.values[which(!is.na <http://is.na>(resp[,1])),c(1,3,5
> )],col=2,type="l",lty=c(1,2,2),ylim=c(0,1))
> lines(t,i*beta_Y)
>
> # Predicted response for Z compared to what I was expecting
> matplot(mod.inla$summary.fitted.values[which(!is.na <http://is.na>(resp[,2])),c(1,3,5
> )],col=4,type="l",lty=c(1,2,2))
> lines(t,i*beta_Z)
>
> # Fitted i_t compared to true i_t
> d<-mod.inla$summary.random$i1[,c(2,4,6)]
> for(j in 1:3) d[,j]<-inv.logit(unlist(d[,j]))
> matplot(d,col=3,type="l",lty=c(1,2,2),ylim=c(0,1))
> lines(t,i)
>
> # beta_Y and beta_Z (I think this is logit-linked?)
> d<-mod.inla$summary.hyperpar[2:3,c(1,3,5)]
> for(j in 1:3) d[,j]<-inv.logit(unlist(d[,j]))
> d
>
> # beta_Y compared to input
> d<-inla.smarginal(mod.inla$marginals.hyperpar$`Beta for i2`)
> d$x<-inv.logit(d$x)
> plot(d,type="l",xlim=c(0,1))
> abline(v=beta_Y,col=2)
>
> # beta_Z compared to input
> d<-inla.smarginal(mod.inla$marginals.hyperpar$`Beta for i3`)
> d$x<-inv.logit(d$x)
> plot(d,type="l",xlim=c(0,1))
> abline(v=beta_Z,col=4)
>
> Thanks in advance for your help and advice! Sorry if I have made some
> obvious mistakes - I am new to using INLA and have never used the

messages.subject_clean: Space-time interaction with Leroux model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am working on the model that I use Leroux (LCAR) for both spatial random effect and space-time interaction  (spatial pattern at each time period). I know the trick of using "Generic1" model to use Leroux for spatial random effect , however I need to know how can I model space-time interaction with LCAR model. Any Help would be appreciated.

Thanks,

Shabnam Balamchi , PhD

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

I seem to have some clues as to what went wrong with the freeze issue. It seems to have something to do with the chosen threshold for calculating the excursion function. Previously, the threshold I was using was a very complicated number dervied from the quantile of the posterior mean of all the pixels, someting like 0.821470329107... But when I changed it to something simpler, like 0.8, there is no freezing. Maybe this explains the weird bug you mentioned. Hope this helps.

Best,
David

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am running LGCP simulation with inlabru and SPDE on a HPC server. But I kept on getting core dump for every simulation that is run. I have contacted support staff of the HPC server about this issue, and they said the problem is from INLA. Below is the result I got after trying to view one of the core files:

$ gdb core core.224843

[New LWP 224843]
Core was generated by `grep ^export'.
Program terminated with signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
#0  0x0000564fdff492a8 in ?? ()

The support staff does not really know what is going on, and I have no idea what is happening here. The code I am running is outputting the result I wanted, so there should not be any program crashing.

Although I can ignore these core dumps, they become a problem if I want to do tens of thousands of simulation. Them being outputted to my remote server directory is likely to cause storage and access problem. Does anyone know what is happening here?

Thanks,
David

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] results of spde functions
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] results of spde functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the M0,M1,M2 matrices in both the inla.sdpe2.matern() and inla.spde2.pcmatern() output objects are internal variables used to setup the model definitions, and are not meant for direct use by users.
The inla.spde2.precision() function knows how to use them to construct the precision matrix for given parameter values (you can look at the code for that function to see how they are used).

inla.barrier.pcmatern() is defined as an generic model, and doesn't use the same internal representation as the "spde2" implementations.
If what you need is a precision matrix, the rgeneric models have methods inside (called Q()) that can produce them, but I'm not sure of the details for how to call those methods.

Finn

Hi Elias,

Thanks for you response. That is interesting that you added  "besagproper2" to capture LCAR model. I do not know why I am getting error. Below is the formula that I am using. Error in inla.interpret.formula(formula, data.same.len = data.same.len,  :

The covariate `RegionID' are used in the following f()-terms: 1, 2
Only one is allowed since the naming convention of the f()-terms depends on unique names of the covariates

You can resolve this as follows:
Not allowed: formula = y ~ f(x, <etc>) + f(x, <etc>) + <etc>

temp <- da2006poly_dbf_adjmat.LHIN

nb2INLA("LHIN1.graph", temp)

adj <- paste(getwd(),"/LHIN1.graph",sep="")

H <- inla.read.graph(filename="LHIN1.graph")

R = -inla.graph2matrix(H)
diag(R) = H$nnbs
n = H$n

###########################
#INLA formula
###########################
formula <- OBS_I ~1+
f(RegionID, model='besagproper2', graph = H, constr=TRUE)+
f(RegionID, model='besagproper2', graph = H, group=timID, control.group=list(model='iid'))

###########################

###########################

model.INLA.Lung.ON<-inla(formula, family="poisson", data=LUNGBincid5yrPrds.NOV2020UP.LHIN_IDs, E=EXP_I,

            control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, quantiles = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)),

            control.compute=list(dic=TRUE),

            control.inla=list(strategy="simplified.laplace"))

###############################

Thanks,

Hi,

the error message states:

"
The covariate `RegionID' are used in the following f()-terms: 1, 2
Only one is allowed since the naming convention of the f()-terms depends on unique names of the covariates
"

This means you need to use a different data column name for each f() model.
Set RegionID2 equal to RegionID in your data object and use f(RegionID,...)+f(RegionID2,...) in the model definition.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear Finn,

I appreciate your response.

In a spatio-temporal model using TMB, the output object of the inla.sdpe2.matern() is used directly to get a precision matrix.
For example,
・grid model; Q = M0*(1+rho^2)^2 + M1*(1+rho^2)*(-rho) + M2*rho^2
・mesh model; the output of R-inla is used in the TMB function to get Q
Because I do not know why we can get Q using M# in grid model, and whether I can use the TMB function using the output of barrier model from R-inla in mesh model, I asked the meaning of M0, M1, and M2.

As you suggested, a precision matrix of barrier model can get using inla.rgeneric.q(), so I get Q in R-inla and give the Q into TMB when I use mesh model. (I think that I can get Q from inla.rgeneric.q() using transformation from dgTMatrix to dgcMatix...?)

Yuki
2021年7月8日木曜日 18:52:18 UTC+9 finn.l...@gmail.com:

> Hi,
>
> the M0,M1,M2 matrices in both the inla.sdpe2.matern() and inla.spde2.pcmatern() output objects are internal variables used to setup the model definitions, and are not meant for direct use by users.
> The inla.spde2.precision() function knows how to use them to construct the precision matrix for given parameter values (you can look at the code for that function to see how they are used).
>
> inla.barrier.pcmatern() is defined as an generic model, and doesn't use the same internal representation as the "spde2" implementations.
> If what you need is a precision matrix, the rgeneric models have methods inside (called Q()) that can produce them, but I'm not sure of the details for how to call those methods.
>
> Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

What you're looking at there are the model parameters, not the fields themselves.
The "group" model means that you're constructing  model where the joint precision is a kronecker product between the spatial and the temporal models.
This means that there is only one spatial parameter in it. If you want different lambda values for each timepoint, you need separate model components for each timepoint.
I see you also had "iid" as group model, which means you were creating independent spatial fields for each time point; this is ok if the aim is to use joint parameters for each timepoint, but it sounds like you might be intending something else?

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Thanks again or your response Finn,

I need to have 4 separate maps for each time periods. This model gives me only two sets of random effects prediction. One for RegionID and another for RegionID1. So how can I have 4 separate maps with only 2 sets of random effects prediction? I checked "summary.random" and it shows only two sets of predictions. here is the code that I am using in Openbugs to get 4 different sets of predictions besides for different lambdas which measure spatial dependency at each time period proportional on the reference time period:

for (i in 1:regions) {

    ins[i]<-b.ins[1]*ins2[i]+b.ins[2]*ins3[i]+b.ins[3]*ins4[i]+b.ins[4]*ins5[i]
    depr[i]<-b.depr[1]*depr2[i]+b.depr[2]*depr3[i]+b.depr[3]*depr4[i]+b.depr[4]*depr5[i]
    dep[i]<-b.dep[1]*dep2[i]+b.dep[2]*dep3[i]+b.dep[3]*dep4[i]+b.dep[4]*dep5[i]
    #eth[i]<-b.eth[1]*eth2[i]+b.eth[2]*eth3[i]+b.eth[3]*eth4[i]+b.eth[4]*eth5[i]

    OBS1[i] ~ dpois(mu[i,1]) # Poisson counts

    log(mu[i,1]) <- logEXP1[i]+beta0+b.Smk*Smk[i]+ins[i]+depr[i]+dep[i]+ b.TP[1]+s1[i]+u[i] # model for mean
    ####

    OBS2[i] ~ dpois(mu[i,2]) # Poisson counts

    log(mu[i,2]) <- logEXP2[i]+beta0+b.Smk*Smk[i]+ins[i]+depr[i]+dep[i]+ b.TP[2]+s2[i]+u[i] # model for mean
    ####

    OBS3[i] ~ dpois(mu[i,3]) # Poisson counts

    log(mu[i,3]) <- logEXP3[i]+beta0+b.Smk*Smk[i]+ins[i]+depr[i]+dep[i]+ b.TP[3]+s3[i]+u[i] # model for mean
    ####

    OBS4[i] ~ dpois(mu[i,4]) # Poisson counts

    log(mu[i,4]) <- logEXP4[i]+beta0+b.Smk*Smk[i]+ins[i]+depr[i]+dep[i]+u[i] # model for mean

  }

  #Prior Distributions:

  # Leroux prior for spatial random effects

  for(k in 1:regions){
    u[k] ~ dnorm(mean.u[k], tau.u[k])
    A[k] <- (rho * num[k] + 1 - rho)
    tau.u[k] <- tau*A[k]
    mean.u[k] <- rho * sum(W.u[cum[k] + 1:cum[k+1]]) / A[k]
  }

  for(h in 1:sumNumNeigh){
    W.u[h] <- u[adj[h]]}

  for(k in 1:regions){
    s1[k] ~ dnorm(mean.s1[k], tau.s1[k])
    B[k] <- (rho.s1 * num[k] + 1 - rho.s1)
    tau.s1[k] <- tau.s.1*B[k]
    mean.s1[k] <- rho.s1 * sum(W.s1[cum[k] + 1:cum[k+1]]) / B[k]
  }

  for(h in 1:sumNumNeigh){
    W.s1[h] <- s1[adj[h]]}

  for(k in 1:regions){
    s2[k] ~ dnorm(mean.s2[k], tau.s2[k])
    C[k] <- (rho.s2 * num[k] + 1 - rho.s2)
    tau.s2[k] <- tau.s.2*C[k]
    mean.s2[k] <- rho.s2 * sum(W.s2[cum[k] + 1:cum[k+1]]) / C[k]
  }

  for(h in 1:sumNumNeigh){
    W.s2[h] <- s2[adj[h]]}

  for(k in 1:regions){
    s3[k] ~ dnorm(mean.s3[k], tau.s3[k])
    D[k] <- (rho.s3 * num[k] + 1 - rho.s3)
    tau.s3[k] <- tau.s.3*D[k]
    mean.s3[k] <- rho.s3 * sum(W.s3[cum[k] + 1:cum[k+1]]) / D[k]
  }

  for(h in 1:sumNumNeigh){
    W.s3[h] <- s3[adj[h]]}

Not sure how can I make it happen with INLA, might be possible with defining four different f()?

Thanks,
Shabnam

> Hi,
>
> What you're looking at there are the model parameters, not the fields themselves.
> The "group" model means that you're constructing  model where the joint precision is a kronecker product between the spatial and the temporal models.
> This means that there is only one spatial parameter in it. If you want different lambda values for each timepoint, you need separate model components for each timepoint.
> I see you also had "iid" as group model, which means you were creating independent spatial fields for each time point; this is ok if the aim is to use joint parameters for each timepoint, but it sounds like you might be intending something else?

> Finn

> > Hi,
> >
> > What you're looking at there are the model parameters, not the fields themselves.
> > The "group" model means that you're constructing  model where the joint precision is a kronecker product between the spatial and the temporal models.
> > This means that there is only one spatial parameter in it. If you want different lambda values for each timepoint, you need separate model components for each timepoint.
> > I see you also had "iid" as group model, which means you were creating independent spatial fields for each time point; this is ok if the aim is to use joint parameters for each timepoint, but it sounds like you might be intending something else?

messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am new to INLA and Bayesian statistics. I'm trying to build up a model. Please let me know if I should provide more information or be more specific!

Right now, I'm trying to fit a model with only age, sex, and year random effects. Then I will add covariates. In the data, there are 2 sexes, 14 age bins and 21 years. There are 51 observations for each age-sex-year combinations (50 US states + DC). To make it faster to experiment with, I took a sample of the data so it has about 3500 observations. I want age groups to be correlated.

form <- y ~ f(as.integer(year), model = "ar1", replicate = as.factor(sex), group = as.integer(age), control.group = list(model = "rw1"))
mod_obj <- inla(formula = form, family = "gaussian", data = dt_sample, control.predictor = list(compute = FALSE, link = 1), control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb"), control.compute = list(config = FALSE, waic = TRUE), verbose = TRUE)

In the output of the model bove, I get a lot of messages like:
file: smtp-taucs.c  1f6a39183ef43d8ef33f10ff3f04fd13f8432758 - Mon Feb 22 21:27:50 2021 +0300
Function: GMRFLib_factorise_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 872, Thread: 0
Fail to factorize Q. I will try to fix it...
It seems I'm poorly specifying the model. Is there some way I could combine age, sex and year or should I break them up?

Thanks so much,
Amal

How spatially dense are the simulated observations? If they’re too far apart then it won’t be able to distinguish between the spatial field and the extra iid effect, and then the priors will be more influential. You probably need to go through your prior specifications and make sure they are reasonable for your problem.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] considering nugget effect
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] considering nugget effect
messages.body_plain:
I agree with Finn that you'll need to check the priors. How large is the estimated range compared to the distances in the data? The estimated sigma is huge for a binomial distribution. The code below illustrated how strong the random effect can be for different baseline values.

install.packages("inlatools", repos = "https://thierryo.r-universe.dev")
library(inlatools)
sims <- simulate_iid(sigma = 2.4)
plot(sims, link = "logit")

I considered this the same as the toy example in  " Advanced Spatial Modeling with Stochastic Partial Differential Equations Using R and INLA " book,
that is considered in the unit square.
pts <- cbind(s1 = sample(1:n / n - 0.5 / n)^2,  s2 = sample(1:n / n - 0.5 / n)^2).
Also, I used the mesh,  inla.spde2.pcmatern and other thing same to this book.
For z ( nugget effect ), I considred the default prior for iid model.

Inlatools it not our package.  You may be able to install it from sources.  Please use R 4.1

—
Haavard Rue
HelpDesk
help@r-inla. org

On 12 Jul 2021, 17:03 +0200, leila.b...@gmail.com <leila.b...@gmail.com>, wrote:

> Thank you for the package that you introduced. I've tried to install this but I got an error.
> package ‘inlatools’ is not available for this version of R
> A version of this package for your version of R might be available elsewhere,
> see the ideas at
> https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-patched/R-admin.html#Installing-packages
>
>
> I tried for R versions 3.6.1, 4.0,  and 4.1.
> What should I do?
>
>
> On Monday, July 12, 2021 at 6:09:51 AM UTC-7 Thierry Onkelinx wrote:
> > I agree with Finn that you'll need to check the priors. How large is the estimated range compared to the distances in the data? The estimated sigma is huge for a binomial distribution. The code below illustrated how strong the random effect can be for different baseline values.
> >
> > install.packages("inlatools", repos = "https://thierryo.r-universe.dev")
> > library(inlatools)
> > sims <- simulate_iid(sigma = 2.4)
> > plot(sims, link = "logit")
> >
> > ir. Thierry Onkelinx
> > Statisticus / Statistician
> >
> > Vlaamse Overheid / Government of Flanders
> > INSTITUUT VOOR NATUUR- EN BOSONDERZOEK / RESEARCH INSTITUTE FOR NATURE AND FOREST
> > Team Biometrie & Kwaliteitszorg / Team Biometrics & Quality Assurance
> > thierry....@inbo.be
> > Havenlaan 88 bus 73, 1000 Brussel
> > www.inbo.be <http://www.inbo.be>
> >
> > ///////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
> > To call in the statistician after the experiment is done may be no more than asking him to perform a post-mortem examination: he may be able to say what the experiment died of. ~ Sir Ronald Aylmer Fisher
> > The plural of anecdote is not data. ~ Roger Brinner
> > The combination of some data and an aching desire for an answer does not ensure that a reasonable answer can be extracted from a given body of data. ~ John Tukey
> > ///////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
> >
> >  <https://www.inbo.be>
> >
> >
> > Op ma 12 jul. 2021 om 14:28 schreef Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com>:
> > > How spatially dense are the simulated observations? If they’re too far apart then it won’t be able to distinguish between the spatial field and the extra iid effect, and then the priors will be more influential. You probably need to go through your prior specifications and make sure they are reasonable for your problem.
> > >
> > > Finn
> > >
> > > > On 12 Jul 2021, at 12:51, leila.b...@gmail.com <leila.b...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > ﻿
> > > > Hi,
> > > > sorry for the late reply.
> > > > I'm in a simulation step. So, I can't find how can I simulate binomial data with spatial effect
> > > > to consider the nugget effect as well, and the result shows the nugget effect.
> > > > the linear predictor is
> > > > eta=1+b*x+u+z,
> > > > where "u" is simulated spatial effect using Matern covariance with nu=1, variance=5, kappa=7.
> > > > "z" is a simulated effect from Normal distribution with mean 0 and sd=0.1 to consider as a nugget effect.
> > > > The summary of result is
> > > > Model hyperparameters:
> > > >                                  mean              sd              0.025quant       0.5quant     0.975quant     mode
> > > > Range for i           5.26e-01        2.73e-01      0.192                 4.62e-01       1.23               0.364

> > > > Precision for z    1.85e+04       1.83e+04     1259.572           1.31e+04      66922.85     3436.917
> > > >
> > > > As you can see the precision for z is big.
> > > >
> > > > Thanks in advance for your help and time.
> > > > Leila
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday, July 8, 2021 at 9:21:29 AM UTC-7 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > Hi,
> > > > >
> > > > > not necessarily a problem; it seems to think that the data doesn't indicate that the extra iid component is needed, which may very well be true, in which case the large precision estimate is appropriate.
> > > > >
> > > > > Finn
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thu, 8 Jul 2021 at 15:14, leila.b...@gmail.com <leila.b...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > Thank you for your quick reply.
> > > > > > I did. The summary of results are here:
> > > > > > Model hyperparameters:
> > > > > >                                  mean       sd              0.025quant    0.5quant    0.975quant     mode
> > > > > > Range for i            4.24e-01 1.99e-01      0.173              3.79e-01   9.34e-01          0.308
> > > > > > Stdev for i             2.60e+00 7.72e-01     1.410              2.49e+00   4.41e+00        2.290
> > > > > > Precision for z     1.84e+04 1.82e+04   1251.757        1.30e+04   6.66e+04       3418.401
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The precision estimation for z (nugget effect) is big and I don't know what's the problem
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Leila
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Thursday, July 8, 2021 at 2:54:06 AM UTC-7 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > if you want to add an iid effect to the predictor for each observation, and "j" is the observation index (1,2,3,...,n) then that looks like the correct formula, yes.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Finn
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Thu, 8 Jul 2021 at 07:40, leila.b...@gmail.com <leila.b...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > Dear INLA group,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I'm going to have nugget effect using SPDE for Binomial family. To do so, I consider
> > > > > > > > extra "iid" model in formula as follows:
> > > > > > > > mu<- 0+beta0+x +f(s, model="spde")+f(j, model="iid").
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I'm in doubt I'm in the correct way or not.
> > > > > > > > If not how can consider the nugget effect in this model?
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Thanks in advance for your help and time.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Leila

messages.subject: SPDE and pseudo-absences
messages.subject_clean: SPDE and pseudo-absences
messages.body_plain:
Dear R-INLA people,

I hope you can help me. I am using INLA to fit a Log Gaussian Cox Process with the SPDE method. I have data of observed animals locations (coded with 1) and pseudo-absences (coded with 0).

The classical SPDE method goes as follows:
1) The observed locations are coded with 1.
2) Create a mesh where the nodes are coded with a 0 and the environmental covariates at the nodes are needed.
3) Create weigths based on the voronoi polygons.
4) Project the mesh to the observed locations
5) Fit the model.

I have found one paper about Species Distribution Modelling (https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12352) where they have observed locations (coded with 1) and pseudo-absences (coded with 0) and they use the INLA-SPDE method to fit their model which goes as follows:

1) The observed locations are coded with 1, the pseudo-absences are coded with 0
2) Create a uniform mesh
3) Project the mesh to the observed locations AND TO THE PSEUDO-ABSENCES
4) The covariates are specified at the observed locations and at the pseudo-absences locations BUT NOT AT THE MESH NODES.
5) The weigths are not based on the voronoi polygons. They are specified as constant weights (spatial_resolution^2)
6) Fit the model

Similar to the mesh nodes, the pseudo-absences are integration points. Thus, Ideally I would like to specify a mesh which nodes are located exactly at the locations of the pseudo-absences and then use the classical SPDE method. However, this leads to completely wrong results. Thus, I have the following questions:

a) Are these pseudo-absences different integration points than the mesh nodes? If no, why is my model leading to wrong results?

b) Is the method presented in the paper also valid if I have pseudo-absences which are not uniformly located in the study area?

c) Is it still possible to use weigths based on the voronoi polygons? If so, how?

Thank you very much and have a nice day!

Best regards,

Rafael

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SPDE and pseudo-absences
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] SPDE and pseudo-absences
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rafael,

this is a good question that often comes up for presence-only data, and the answer is a bit complex, and depends on precisely how the "pseudo-absences" are constructed/chosen/invented.

1) If both presences and absences were observed at specific locations, then the natural observation model would be a Bernoulli model at those locations (Bin(1,p))
2) If the presences were obtained through complete search of a region (optionally with imperfect but model-able detection probability) then the natural model
would be a Log Gaussian Cox process, where the likelihood involves a sum over the log-intensity at the presences, and subtracting the integral of the intensity over the entire region.

For case 2, we can implement that for mesh based spde predictors by using a numerical integration scheme. In order for the resulting likelihood approximation to be stable,
the integration scheme must not fail to counterbalance the sum in the likelihood. Such failure can lead it to estimate infinite intensity at the absences, and zero intensity elsewhere.
For this reason, the safest integration scheme is one that places integration points at all mesh nodes, since that "surrounds" any possible presence, and ensures the likelihood doesn't degenerate.
In case the mesh is chosen to have mesh nodes coinciding with presences, one could conceivably be a bit more flexible as long as one also has integration points at those nodes, but that mostly
leads to the same integration points; placing them at the mesh nodes.

In this general LGCP approximation, one may use the voronoi cells around each mesh node as integration point, but that's a 0-order approximation of the integral (i.e. piecewise constant intensity around each mesh node). If we instead build an integration scheme based on the basis functions in the mesh, we get a higher order approximation of the continuous domain model. Both are valid approaches, but the automated implementation in the inlabru interface lgcp() function uses the higher order approximation.

Now we get to the presence-only case:
3) If we only have presences, but for some reason an LGCP is _not_ the natural true model, but we invent pseudo-absences in order to mimic the LGCP likelihood discussed above.
However, unless the pseudo-absences and associated weights are chosen appropriately, it may not be a valid likelihood model.
(Note: it's not always clear to me when this is appropriate; for cases where an actual LGCP _is_ the appropriate model, one should go back to the fundamentals and not prematurely invent pseudo-absences. And when an LGCP is _not_ the appropriate model, then the entire construction relies on the pseudo-absences&weights _defining_ an appropriate model structure.)

The problem is that _if_ the intensity field is determined only by large scale covariates that vary slowly over space, then the pseudo-absences and related weights can provide a stable likelihood expression, since changing the covariate weights affects the whole field, and the degenerate case discussed above will typically not happen. But when we introduce a Gaussian field into the log-intensity, that's no longer the case, and all the issues discussed above return.
In the paper you linked, they appear to get around the issue by always including the presence locations as pseudo-absences (see eqn 5, where the presences are included in the integral approximation).
Thus, as mentioned above for integration points coinciding with mesh nodes, if they choose the weights appropriately, this can yield a valid stable likelihood expression, and just need enough integration points to resolve the needed spatial scales of the Gaussian field.
How appropriate such a model is depends on the application and how the weights are chosen.

But in all the cases above, the covariates need to be available for every location where there is either an observation or an integration point.
So if you make an integration scheme that doesn't include the mesh nodes, that should be ok, _if_ the other requirements on a stable likelihood model are fulfilled, as discussed above.

The main issues seem to be
1) how to choose the pseudo-absence weights for the presence locations, and
2) how to choose the pseudo-absence weights for the other pseudo-absence integration points.

I couldn't immediately see how they differentiate between those two types of points when choosing the weights, but the reason for constant weights seems to be that they used a uniform grid of integration points, in which case the grid cells _are_ the voronoi sets. However, that doesn't quite work if the presence locations also need integration weights. If they set those to zero, then they only get a stable integration scheme if it's dense enough in space.

In summary, the issues are that
1) presence-only data doesn't necessarily have a well-defined observation likelihood model
2) _If_ one assumes it can be modelled with an LGCP model, one needs to ensure a stable likelihood approximation, and "pseudo-absence" is just a fancy word for "location of a point in a numerical integration scheme", and going back to how to construct valid integral approximations provides solutions to the problem.
3) Such an approximation may be more or less appropriate, depending on how the weights at presences are chosen, and how the weights at pseudo-absences are chosen (including cases that are specifically _not_ approximations of a well-defined LGCP, but instead a model solely _defined_ by the pseudo-absences and weights).

Related references that discuss the case when an LGCP _is_ the model, but not the special presence-only situation:
https://academic.oup.com/biomet/article/103/1/49/2389990
https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-applied-statistics/volume-11/issue-4/Point-process-models-for-spatio-temporal-distance-sampling-data-from/10.1214/17-AOAS1078.full

Best wishes,
Finn

> > For this reason, the safest integration scheme is one that places integration points at all mesh nodes, since that "surrounds" any possible presence, and ensures the likelihood doesn't degenerate.
> > In case the mesh is chosen to have mesh nodes coinciding with presences, one could conceivably be a bit more flexible as long as one also has integration points at those nodes, but that mostly
> > leads to the same integration points; placing them at the mesh nodes.
> >
> > In this general LGCP approximation, one may use the voronoi cells around each mesh node as integration point, but that's a 0-order approximation of the integral (i.e. piecewise constant intensity around each mesh node). If we instead build an integration scheme based on the basis functions in the mesh, we get a higher order approximation of the continuous domain model. Both are valid approaches, but the automated implementation in the inlabru interface lgcp() function uses the higher order approximation.
> >
> > Now we get to the presence-only case:
> > 3) If we only have presences, but for some reason an LGCP is _not_ the natural true model, but we invent pseudo-absences in order to mimic the LGCP likelihood discussed above.
> > However, unless the pseudo-absences and associated weights are chosen appropriately, it may not be a valid likelihood model.
> > (Note: it's not always clear to me when this is appropriate; for cases where an actual LGCP _is_ the appropriate model, one should go back to the fundamentals and not prematurely invent pseudo-absences. And when an LGCP is _not_ the appropriate model, then the entire construction relies on the pseudo-absences&weights _defining_ an appropriate model structure.)
> >
> > The problem is that _if_ the intensity field is determined only by large scale covariates that vary slowly over space, then the pseudo-absences and related weights can provide a stable likelihood expression, since changing the covariate weights affects the whole field, and the degenerate case discussed above will typically not happen. But when we introduce a Gaussian field into the log-intensity, that's no longer the case, and all the issues discussed above return.
> > In the paper you linked, they appear to get around the issue by always including the presence locations as pseudo-absences (see eqn 5, where the presences are included in the integral approximation).
> > Thus, as mentioned above for integration points coinciding with mesh nodes, if they choose the weights appropriately, this can yield a valid stable likelihood expression, and just need enough integration points to resolve the needed spatial scales of the Gaussian field.
> > How appropriate such a model is depends on the application and how the weights are chosen.
> >
> > But in all the cases above, the covariates need to be available for every location where there is either an observation or an integration point.
> > So if you make an integration scheme that doesn't include the mesh nodes, that should be ok, _if_ the other requirements on a stable likelihood model are fulfilled, as discussed above.
> >
> > The main issues seem to be
> > 1) how to choose the pseudo-absence weights for the presence locations, and
> > 2) how to choose the pseudo-absence weights for the other pseudo-absence integration points.
> >
> > I couldn't immediately see how they differentiate between those two types of points when choosing the weights, but the reason for constant weights seems to be that they used a uniform grid of integration points, in which case the grid cells _are_ the voronoi sets. However, that doesn't quite work if the presence locations also need integration weights. If they set those to zero, then they only get a stable integration scheme if it's dense enough in space.
> >
> > In summary, the issues are that
> > 1) presence-only data doesn't necessarily have a well-defined observation likelihood model
> > 2) _If_ one assumes it can be modelled with an LGCP model, one needs to ensure a stable likelihood approximation, and "pseudo-absence" is just a fancy word for "location of a point in a numerical integration scheme", and going back to how to construct valid integral approximations provides solutions to the problem.
> > 3) Such an approximation may be more or less appropriate, depending on how the weights at presences are chosen, and how the weights at pseudo-absences are chosen (including cases that are specifically _not_ approximations of a well-defined LGCP, but instead a model solely _defined_ by the pseudo-absences and weights).
> >
> > Related references that discuss the case when an LGCP _is_ the model, but not the special presence-only situation:
> > https://academic.oup.com/biomet/article/103/1/49/2389990
> > https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-applied-statistics/volume-11/issue-4/Point-process-models-for-spatio-temporal-distance-sampling-data-from/10.1214/17-AOAS1078.full
> >
> > Best wishes,
> > Finn
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Wed, 14 Jul 2021 at 11:12, rafa.arc...@gmail.com <rafa.arc...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Dear R-INLA people,
> > >
> > > I hope you can help me. I am using INLA to fit a Log Gaussian Cox Process with the SPDE method. I have data of observed animals locations (coded with 1) and pseudo-absences (coded with 0).
> > >
> > > The classical SPDE method goes as follows:
> > > 1) The observed locations are coded with 1.
> > > 2) Create a mesh where the nodes are coded with a 0 and the environmental covariates at the nodes are needed.
> > > 3) Create weigths based on the voronoi polygons.
> > > 4) Project the mesh to the observed locations
> > > 5) Fit the model.
> > >
> > > I have found one paper about Species Distribution Modelling (https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12352) where they have observed locations (coded with 1) and pseudo-absences (coded with 0) and they use the INLA-SPDE method to fit their model which goes as follows:

messages.subject: Variable selection in INLA - PC priors
messages.subject_clean: Variable selection in INLA - PC priors
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm modeling spatial (areal) data. Dataset has ~50 covariates with moderate multicollinearity. I wanted to test some shrinkage/regularization approach to deal with high dimensionality and multicollinearity and this led me to the PC priors.

But as I understand it (maybe I'm wrong), PC priors' main use is not variable selection. Under section 4.5 Sparsity priors of Simpson et al (2017) <https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.4630> I read that the exponential PC prior is not suited for variable selection and that the half-Cauchy prior might. But then I found that Dan Simpson does not recommend half-Cauchy prior for the std. dev. <https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2018/04/03/justify-my-love/>

So I'm a bit confused. My questions are:

1. Can I use PC priors for variable selection in hierarchical bayesian models?
2. If yes, are they implemented in INLA? (Example would be great)
3. If not, which approach would you recommend to do variable selection/regularization in INLA?

Thank you very much!

Hi Finn,

I have checked the covariate, it is certainly not 1. The code for model definition is provided below:

#normalize covariate
cov_gal$z <- cov_gal$z - mean(cov_gal$z, na.rm = TRUE)

f.gal <- function(x, y) {
  # turn coordinates into SpatialPoints object:
  # with the appropriate coordinate reference system (CRS)
  spp <- SpatialPoints(data.frame(x = x, y = y), proj4string = fm_sp_get_crs(cov_gal))
  proj4string(spp) <- fm_sp_get_crs(cov_gal)
  # Extract elevation values at spp coords, from our elev SpatialGridDataFrame
  v <- over(spp, cov_gal)
  if (any(is.na <http://is.na>(v$z))) {
    v$z <- inlabru:::bru_fill_missing(cov_gal, spp, v$z)
  }
  return(v$z)
}

#point pattern
spv <- SpatialPoints(v_acs[,3:4])

#mesh
v_mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = spv, boundary = region,
                       max.edge = c(80, 800), cutoff = 40, max.n.strict = 1300L)

#spde model
v_spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = v_mesh, alpha = 1.5,
                              prior.range = c(2000, 0.975),
                              prior.sigma = c(1.5, 0.5))

#model components
cmp <- coordinates ~ gal(f.gal(x, y), model = "linear") + f(coordinates, model = v_spde) + Intercept(1)
spv <- SpatialPointsDataFrame(spv, data = data.frame(id = rep(1, nrow(as.data.frame(spv)))))

fit <- lgcp(cmp, spv,
            samplers = region,
            domain = list(coordinates = v_mesh),
            options = list(control.inla=list(int.strategy = 'ccd'),
                           control.compute=list(config=TRUE),
                           control.results=list(return.marginals.random = TRUE,
                                                return.marginals.predictor = TRUE),
                           control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE)))

Thanks,
David

I have been scheduling large sets of INLA models on a large compute cluster. Scheduling and resource allocation are done via SLURM (if that matters). I'm running models with 24 cores each, ~1.5GB memory/core. I seem to have squashed all the seg faults and other errors. Now, it just returns "done" within the output file and ends. In the error file, it reports "killed" with no other details.

Here's the contents of my SLURM error file:
Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.
Calls: inla -> inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed
In addition: Warning message:
In inla.model.properties.generic(inla.trim.family(model), mm[names(mm) ==  :
  Model 'z' in section 'latent' is marked as 'experimental'; changes may appear at any time.
  Use this model with extra care!!! Further warnings are disabled.
Execution halted

I am running INLA with debug=TRUE (and debugging turned on via the environment variable), and I am using pardiso. Pardiso returns a few errors: *** PARDISO ERROR(0): not pos.def matrix: 15 eigenvalues are negative.
*** PARDISO ERROR: I will try to work around the problem...

But these seem not to be catastrophic. The level is a nested model similar to the one in chapter 4 of Gomez-Rubio 2020.

I am at a bit of a loss as the output from SLURM contains absolutely no errors (aside from the above PARDISO ERROR) and no other memory or resource related issues. I'm happy to post any other useful information.

Thanks for your time and help.
Scott

messages.body_plain:
I think the first to check if this runs without SLURM in interactive
mode, as then the crashes with due to 'slurm' / running in batch mode

the 'not pos.def matrix' is usually due to ill conditioned matrix, most
often again, due to vague model and not that informative data. tips here
is setting

	control.fixed=list(prec=1,prec.intercept=1)

or similar.

you can also try the newest testing version you get with R-4.1 and then
add option inla.mode="experimental"

let me know
H

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your advice - perhaps instead of seeing the data as event (1/0) plus time to event (for status = 0) I could use a hurdle model, with a binomial probability of the event, and some other distribution for time to event? E.g. negative binomial.

A sample R script for a hurdle model has been kindly contributed by Elias Krainski (https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/DPvHIGcbd0E/m/etxPf7JeAQAJ)

...where it seems we have a two-column response variable where NAs are introduced to show where the binomial result = 0.

Does that make it impossible to do predictions the usual way? (I mean by supplying the new data predictors, coding the response variable as NA, and fitting the old and new data together). Or can I supply both response variables as NA, will that be interpreted as 'new data'? e.g.
 z       y
 1      7
 0     NA
NA   NA [new data to make prediction for]

Otherwise, I suppose I'll be needing 'inla.posterior.sample' here too?

> regression. for simple models, this conversion is done automatic, but

>
> if a response is NA, then there is no (easy) way to predict a new
> outcome as the poisson expansion is done based on the observed value.
> you may have to do the prediction manually, using
> 'inla.posterior.sample', f.ex, to get a sample of the hazard function

messages.subject: Poisson with non-integer data
messages.subject_clean: Poisson with non-integer data
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

We have an area divided into smaller parts. We counted the number of animals in each of the parts. In some parts we used one method, in other parts a second method. The goal is to see whether the methods yield a different observed density. So the model is quite simple.

inla(
  count ~ part_area + method + f(part, model = "iid"), family = poisson,
  control.fixed = list(
    mean = c(part_area = 1, default = 0),
    prec = c(part_area = 1000, default = 0.001
  )
)

The problem is that some animals have their home range in two neighbouring parts. Or partly outside the study area. Attributing a fraction of the count to the part leads to non-integer counts, making the Poisson distribution invalid.

Suppose that a part gets a count of 3.2. An idea is to split the observation into two observations.? One with count 3 and weight 0.8 and the second with count 4 and weight 0.2. And then apply a Poisson distribution with a weighted log-likelihood (using the weights argument). Does this make sense? Is there a better way of doing this?

Best regards,

ir. Thierry Onkelinx
Statisticus / Statistician

Vlaamse Overheid / Government of Flanders
INSTITUUT VOOR NATUUR- EN BOSONDERZOEK / RESEARCH INSTITUTE FOR NATURE AND FOREST
Team Biometrie & Kwaliteitszorg / Team Biometrics & Quality Assurance

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Poisson with non-integer data
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Poisson with non-integer data
messages.body_plain:
Hi THierry,

whether the fractional splitting and log-likelihood weighting itself is the best approach to the problem is a longer story (e.g. can it be formulated as a model that is motivated directly by a data generating process for your situation), but when it comes to implementing it, there is a shortcut: If you have weights w1 and w2 such that w1+w2=1 and y=w1 y1 + w2 y2 (as in your example), then the weighted log-likelihood for intensity lambda becomes

w1 y1 log(lambda) - w1 lambda + w2 y2 log(lambda) - w2 lambda - w1 log(y1!) - w2 log(y2!)
  = (w1 y1 + w2 y2) log(lambda) - (w1 + w2) lambda - w1 log(y1!) - w2 log(y2!)
  = y log(lambda) - lambda - w1 log(y1!) - w2 log(y2!)

Only the y-factorial terms and the fact that y can be fractional distinguishes this from a regular Poisson model.
R-INLA implements the "xpoisson" model, that implements the log-likelihood

  y log(lambda) - lambda - log(floor(y)!)

for non-integer y-values.

Apart from the factorial terms, that's identical to the weighted log-likelihood model construction.
The difference in the normalisation constant means you need to be careful about using the likelihood values for comparisons with different data values (this is also true for weighted log-likelihoods)

See inla.doc("xpoisson") for some more information (it's in the same document as the regular "poisson" model).

Finn

messages.subject: Spatially varying coefficient model - fail to factorize Q
messages.subject_clean: Spatially varying coefficient model - fail to factorize Q
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to run a spatially varying logistic regression model with large data (1.6 million individuals nested in 16500 geographic units. The model is specified as follows:

SVC <- inla(y ~  1 +
              x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 +
              f(idx2, x6, model = "besag", constr=FALSE,
                graph = "graph", scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.001)))) +
              f(idx3, x7, model = "besag", constr=FALSE,
                graph = " graph  ", scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.001)))) +
              f(idx4, x8, model = "besag", constr=FALSE,
                graph = " graph  ", scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.001)))) +
              f(idx5, x9, model = "besag", constr=FALSE,
                graph = " graph  ", scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.001)))) ,
            family = "binomial",  control.family = list(link = "logit"), data=sample,
            control.compute = list(dic=T, openmp.strategy = "huge"),
            control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb", reordering = "amdc"), verbose = T)

where y is my dependent variable and x1 .... x9 are my explanatory variables.

However, I get the following errors:

file: smtp-taucs.c  hgid: 8b30e851fed2  date: Tue Mar 17 10:38:12 2020 +0300
Function: GMRFLib_factorise_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 876, Thread: 0
Fail to factorize Q. I will try to fix it...

max.logdens= -53147.9462 fn= 12 theta= 4.9494 4.0103 4.0007 4.3136 4.0041  range=[-11.82 1.22]
max.logdens= -53116.3134 fn= 13 theta= 4.9594 4.0103 3.9907 4.3136 4.0041  range=[-11.84 1.21]

file: smtp-taucs.c  hgid: 8b30e851fed2  date: Tue Mar 17 10:38:12 2020 +0300
Function: GMRFLib_factorise_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 876, Thread: 0
Fail to factorize Q. I will try to fix it...

What can I do to get INLA to factorize Q?

Many thanks in advance!

Best, Boris

the issue is a numerical singular (precision) matrix. please check that
the covariates x1, x2, ... are properly scaled

you may try the most recent testing version (which require R-4.1), and
add

	inla(..., inla.mode="experimental")

this should use less RAM and be more suited to this type of model.

it might give you some errors in the options (as not all options are
allowed), but just remove those it complains about and use default

if this is still an issue, please send me code & data to rerun here to
help@...

thx
H

messages.subject: Frailty survival model - Regions with no data
messages.subject_clean: Frailty survival model - Regions with no data
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am running a survival model with cases nested in regions. The definition of my cohort means some regions in the study country has no information for both the outcome and covariates. Approximately half of the 2210 regions has no data however i wanted to get estimates for the regions with no data.

I defined my formula as

form <- inla.surv(time, outcome) + 1 + x1 ... + xn + f(ID, model="iid")

I want to know if the estimates from the regions with no data would be reliable considering it is an iid model or should I use bym model instead of the former (iid).

Thank you.

messages.subject: Estimation results differ when adding points for prediction
messages.subject_clean: Estimation results differ when adding points for prediction
messages.body_plain:
Dear all

I am rather new to INLA and following loosely "Advanced spatial modelling with spde using R and INLA". When I estimate a model with an estimation stack, I obtain slightly different estimates as if I estimate the model with a joint stack composed of the same estimation stack and a prediction stack. This seems very counterintuitive to me, since the data for estimation are the same. Why is this?

I include a rather lengthy reprex: Why do the last three lines not yield the exact same results?

rm(list = ls())
library(INLA)
library(tidyverse)

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(
  loc.domain =  cbind(c(0,0,1,1), c(0,1,1,0)),
  max.edge = c(0.1, 0.2))
plot(mesh)

spde <- mesh %>%
  inla.spde2.pcmatern(alpha = 2,
                      prior.range = c(0.3,0.5),
                      prior.sigma = c(10, 0.01))
data("SPDEtoy")
toy1 <- SPDEtoy %>%
  sf::st_as_sf(
    coords = c("s1", "s2"),
    crs = "+proj=utm +zone=19 +datum=NAD83 +units=m +no_defs +ellps=GRS80
+towgs84=0,0,0"
  )
coords <- toy1 %>%
  sf::st_coordinates()

# Estimation --------------------------------------------------------------
A_est <- mesh %>%
  inla.spde.make.A(loc = coords)
A_est %>% dim
stack_est <- inla.stack(
  data = list(resp = toy1$y),
  A = list(A_est,1),
  effects = list(i = 1:spde$n.spde,
                 beta0 = rep(1, nrow(toy1))),
  tag = "est"
)

stack_est %>%
  inla.stack.A() %>%
  dim()

res_est <- inla(resp ~0 + beta0 + f(i, model = spde),
            data = inla.stack.data(stack_est),
            control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack_est)))

# Prediction Method1 ------------------------------------------------------
pred_grid <- expand.grid(x= seq(0, 1, length.out = 101),
                         y= seq(0, 1, length.out = 101)) %>%
  as.matrix()
A_pred <- mesh %>%
  inla.spde.make.A(loc = pred_grid)

stack_pred <- inla.stack(
  data = list(resp = NA),
  A = list(A_pred, 1),
  effects = list(i = 1:spde$n.spde, beta0 = rep(1, 101 * 101)),
  tag = "pred"
)

stack_join <- inla.stack(stack_est, stack_pred)

res_pred <- inla(resp ~0 + beta0 + f(i, model = spde),
                 data = inla.stack.data(stack_join),
                 control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack_join)))

# Prediction Method2 ------------------------------------------------------
pgrid0 <- inla.mesh.projector(mesh, xlim = 0:1, ylim = 0:1, dims=c(101, 101))
stack_pred_proj <- inla.stack(
  data = list(resp = NA),
  A = list(pgrid0$proj$A, 1),
  effects = list(i = 1:spde$n.spde, beta0 = rep(1, 101 * 101)),
  tag = "pred_proj"
)
stack_join1 <- inla.stack(stack_est, stack_pred_proj)
res_pred_proj <- inla(resp ~0 + beta0 + f(i, model = spde),
                 data = inla.stack.data(stack_join1),
                 control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack_join1)))

# Results Comparison ------------------------------------------------------
res_est %>% summary()
res_pred %>% summary()
res_pred_proj %>% summary()

Cheers, Dan

messages.subject: Pre-computing graph in INLA?
messages.subject_clean: Pre-computing graph in INLA?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to run a rather large model (N~1million) fitting a covariance matrix that's size NxN. The covariance matrix describes the relatedness between individuals and is positive definite and quite sparse. For smaller problems INLA runs nicely and fast. The model is,

prec_ord <- inla.qreordering(Ainv, 'metis')
model <- inla(y ~ 1 + f(IID, model='generic0', hyper=list(theta=prec.A), constr = TRUE, Cmatrix=Ainv), family = 'binomial', data=newdat, verbose=TRUE, num.threads = 1,
control.inla=(reordering=prec_ord)

However, there is quite a long setup step in before INLA gets to "Size of graph" that takes ~1h. (see below). Is there any way to speed up this step by pre-calculating the graph, or similar? I'm currently experimenting with different priors and other options to see how it affects the estimates, so waiting ~1h for the same data set over and over seems slightly excessive. I've tried to pre-calculate the ordering using inla.qordering but that does not affect it al all.

inla_INLA...
Sparse-matrix library.... [pardiso]
OpenMP strategy.......... [pardiso]
num.threads.............. [1:1]
blas.num.threads......... [1]
Density-strategy......... [Low]
----> Takes ~1h before it prints size of graph
Size of graph............ [1999999]
Number of constraints.... [1]

Thanks in advance,
David

have some spatial pattern, then you might want to consider a different
model (like some regional model often used for disease mapping)

> Dear all

> since the data for estimation are the same. Why is this?

> yield the exact same results?
>
> rm(list = ls())

> plot(mesh)
>
> spde <- mesh %>%
>   inla.spde2.pcmatern(alpha = 2,
>                       prior.range = c(0.3,0.5),
>                       prior.sigma = c(10, 0.01))
> data("SPDEtoy")
> toy1 <- SPDEtoy %>%
>   sf::st_as_sf(
>     coords = c("s1", "s2"),
>     crs = "+proj=utm +zone=19 +datum=NAD83 +units=m +no_defs
> +ellps=GRS80

>
> # Estimation ---------------------------------------------------------
> -----

>   inla.spde.make.A(loc = coords)
> A_est %>% dim

>   effects = list(i = 1:spde$n.spde,

>

>

messages.body_plain:
make sure you use the most recent testing version (and R-4.1), and I
have seen METIS-4.1 take an insane long time for some examples, but the
METIS-5 version is much much quicker. at some point I realized that
METIS-4 was used and not METIS-5, as I thought METIS-5 was default but
it was not.

Let me know if this does not work out.

while you're at it, you might throw in option

	inla(..., inla.mode="experimental")

see NEWS. hopefully this will run faster and with less RAM requirement

H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Variable selection in INLA - PC priors
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Variable selection in INLA - PC priors
messages.body_plain:
sorry for late reply.

yes, the pc priors were never designed for variable selection of ``fixed
effects'', but we had more in model other type of hyperparameters
elsewhere in the model.

I agree with Dan that the pc-prior for stdev is a natural starting point
and this is what the pc-priors say it should be. I also agree that the
half-Cauchy is 'to much', and there were no strong justification for it
in the first place (it was kind of ``think of a number''), and the tails
are simply to heavy and it did not made any sense to me.

INLA does not implement variable selection, but you have to use multiple
runs and compare 'manually' either by some criteria, or by the (log)
marginal likelihood

Best
H

> sorry for late reply.
>
>
> yes, the pc priors were never designed for variable selection of ``fixed
> effects'', but we had more in model other type of hyperparameters
> elsewhere in the model.
>
> I agree with Dan that the pc-prior for stdev is a natural starting point
> and this is what the pc-priors say it should be. I also agree that the
> half-Cauchy is 'to much', and there were no strong justification for it
> in the first place (it was kind of ``think of a number''), and the tails
> are simply to heavy and it did not made any sense to me.
>
> INLA does not implement variable selection, but you have to use multiple
> runs and compare 'manually' either by some criteria, or by the (log)
> marginal likelihood
>

messages.subject: Checking on the parameterization of a negative binomial with mean dispersion - "NB2"
messages.subject_clean: Checking on the parameterization of a negative binomial with mean dispersion - "NB2"
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am currently using R-INLA for my MSc dissertation, as it is very flexible and accessible when fitting spatial/spatio-temporal (S/ST) models. Working up to S/ST models I fit multi-level models, one in a frequentist framework using Stata (menbreg function using log link, https://www.stata.com/manuals14/memenbreg.pdf), as it seemed to be the only program where the model would converge, and I would like to fit another in R-INLA motivating the use of it in further chapters. However, when I fit the model, I get markedly different results that are difficult for me to reason with - could it be due to model identifiability?  Or is it just me not aligning my model specification with Stata's?

I have count data that may normally be modelled assuming a Poisson distribution, but due to the presence of over-dispersion, I've opted for a negative binomial distribution, with dispersion parameterized in terms of the mean accounting for an offset. My data is hierarchical in nature with 5 repeated annual measurements of prescription rates recorded for GP offices nested within higher-level health authorities (i.e., a 3-level model). Thus, I'd like to include random effects (intercepts) for the GP offices and higher-level health authorities; I will add a spatially structured component later on at the health authority level. I am interested in modelling the prescribing rate per 1000 patients, so my offset is log(number of patients/1000). However, from reading the nbinomial R-INLA documentation, perhaps I should specify the exposure E as (number of patients/1000) and variant=1 in the control.family argument to get dispersion modelled in terms of the mean accounting for a different offset i for every observation as Stata does, and not assuming constant over-dispersion as it seems variant=0 does. That said, it seems I shouldn't have offset=log(number of patients/1000), but instead use the E argument. Please see some sample code below, with no adjustment to priors, so I wouldn't expect the estimates to be so different (the factor variable and the intercept are where the estimates differ the most):

formula.modeMLM = NumItems ~ 1  + CPercHyp + CPercOB + yrc + yrc2 +             CGPHeadcount + factor(IMDScoreQuintile_LOCF) +
                    f(CCG_ID, model="iid") + #Health Authority/CCG
                    f(CCG_ORG, model="iid") #GP office/practice

resultsMLM = inla(formula.modeMLM, family="nbinomial", data=MLM , E=patsper1000,                               control.family=list(link='log', variant=1),
                           control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic=TRUE))

Is there anything that just seems wrong in my specification leading to different estimates, or is Stata's specification just not possible in R-INLA, thus, I can simply say they differ because they are not exactly the same parameterization (see attached Stata's write-up on how they parameterize over-dispersion)? Happy to share data.

Thank you for reading my post and any help is appreciated!
Nick

messages.body_plain:
this seemingly easy task, to make sure to are comparing the results of
*the same model*,  is surprising difficult in pratice. Especially
neg.binomial has several parameterisation. INLA use (see ?rnbinom)

     An alternative parametrization (often used in ecology) is by the
     _mean_ ‘mu’ (see above), and ‘size’, the _dispersion parameter_,
     where ‘prob’ = ‘size/(size+mu)’.  The variance is ‘mu + mu^2/size’
     in this parametrization.

see inla.doc('nbinomial') for details.

one way towards this, is to do a comparison with Gaussian data with
fixed precision, like

	inla(...,
		family="gaussian",
		control.family=list(hyper=list(prec=list(initial=0,fixe
d=TRUE))))

as then the computations should be exact (up to numerical integration).

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I have a Bernoulli space-time model and am trying to plot the spatial random fields. However, I keep getting stuck.

Here is my code:

#I have 3 years of data
NYear <- length(unique(datafile.final2$YearSeq))

#create the mesh
mesh2 <- inla.mesh.create.helper(points=cbind(datafile.final2$x, datafile.final2$y),max.edge=c(20000,40000), cutoff=4000)

coords <- as.matrix(datafile.final2[,1:2])

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh2, alpha=2)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh2, loc=coords,group=datafile.final2$YearSeq,n.group = NYear)

time.index <- inla.spde.make.index("w", n.spde=spde$n.spde,n.group = NYear)

N <- nrow(datafile.final2)

X <- data.frame(Intercept=rep(1,N), datafile.final2$Phos.std,datafile.final2$salinity.std,datafile.final2$total.area.std, datafile.final2$distance.to.edge.std,datafile.final2$distance.between.beds.std,datafile.final2$bath.std)

colnames(X) <- c("Intercept","Phos.std","salinity.std","total.area.std", "distance.to.edge.std","distance.between.beds.std", "bath.std")

stack3 <- inla.stack(data=list(y=datafile.final2$pres, link=1,Ntrials=1),A=list(A,1),effects=list(w=time.index, X=as.data.frame(X)), tag="est")

hyper <- list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.01)))

formula3 <- y ~ -1 + Intercept + Phos.std+salinity.std+total.area.std + distance.to.edge.std+distance.between.beds.std + bath.std+f(w, model=spde,group=w.group,control.group = list(model="ar1",scale.model = T),hyper=hyper)

data = inla.stack.data(stack3)

r3 <- inla(formula3, control.inla=list(reordering="metis"),family="binomial",Ntrials=1, data=data, control.compute=list(dic=T,cpo=T,config=T),control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack3), compute=T, link=1, quantiles=c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)),control.fixed=list(prec.intercept = 0.1))

#my attempt at prediction of the random field
w.pm <http://w.pm> <- r3$summary.random$coordinates$mean

projgrid <- inla.mesh.projector(mesh2, xlim=range(datafile.final2$x),ylim=range(datafile.final2$y))

#for loop for 3 years
xmean <- list()
for (j in 1:3)
  xmean[[j]] <- inla.mesh.project(
    projgrid, r3$summary.random$w$mean[time.index$w.group == j])

I'm just not sure where to go from here to plot the spatial fields!

I have no trouble getting the overall predictions by year; I would like to generate a plot something like this (see attached; which brings me to another question-is there a way to convert this plot from what I assume are log odds to probabilities?):

#overall predictions
idx <- inla.stack.data(stack3, tag = "pred")
preds <- r3$summary.linear.predictor
datafile.final2$pred <- preds$mean[1:nrow(datafile.final2)]
lattice::levelplot(pred ~ x + y|YearSeq, data = datafile.final2)

Thank you very much!!
-Carrie

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Here's an example for using ggplot, adapted from https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/web/2d_lgcp_plotsampling.html
The masking of the region requires you have the boundary as a SpatialPolygons object.
Otherwise it will show the whole mesh.
First a basic example, then one where I've tried to use your variables.

# Load inlabru
library(inlabru)
library(ggplot2)

# Generic example, with colors taken from the mesh coordinates (just to have something to plot):
mesh<-inla.mesh.2d(cbind(0,0),offset = 1, max.edge=0.1)

# Alt 1: Let inlabru::gg handle the conversion from mesh to pixels:
ggplot()+gg(mesh, color=mesh$loc[,1])

# Alt 2: Do your own conversion to pixels:
pix<-pixels(mesh)
proj <- inla.mesh.projector(mesh, coordinates(pix))
pix[["A"]] <- inla.mesh.project(proj, mesh$loc[,1])
pix[["B"]] <- inla.mesh.project(proj, mesh$loc[,2])
ggplot()+gg(pix, aes(fill=A))
ggplot()+gg(pix, aes(fill=B))

# Both side-by side with correct aspect ratio and common legend:
library(patchwork)
(ggplot()+gg(mesh, color=mesh$loc[,1]) |
 ggplot()+gg(mesh, color=mesh$loc[,2])) +
  coord_fixed() +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "right") &
  scale_fill_continuous()

# Alt 1:
ggplot() +
  gg(mesh2, color = r3$summary.random$w$mean[time.index$w.group == j],
     nx = 300, ny =300, mask = boundary)

# Alt 2:
pix <- pixels(mesh2, mask = boundary)
gproj <- inla.mesh.projector(mesh2, coordinates(pix))
for (j in 1:3) {
  pix[[paste0("mean", j)]] <- inla.mesh.project(

    gproj, r3$summary.random$w$mean[time.index$w.group == j])
}

ggplot() + gg(pix, aes(fill = mean1))

# All three side-by side with patchwork and common legend:
library(patchwork)
(ggplot() + gg(pix, aes(fill = mean1)) |
  ggplot() + gg(pix, aes(fill = mean2)) |
  ggplot() + gg(pix, aes(fill = mean3))) +
  coord_fixed() +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") &
  scale_fill_continuous()

Finn
